paras: The Huntsville mob beatings of May 1919 were assaults on five Black men by a mob near Huntsville, Walker County, Texas, on May 26, 1919, during a search for a Black man a white schoolgirl said she had seen behind an abandoned house. The girl said none of the men brought before her was the one she saw, but the mob beat all of them, left Ed Morgan unconscious, and threatened to kill his family. The Houston Informer gave the attack a front-page banner; the Baltimore Afro-American condensed it a week later.

According to the Informer's Huntsville correspondent, a 16-year-old white schoolgirl alleged that she had seen a Black man coming from the rear of an abandoned house "buttoning up his trousers," and an effort was made "to apprehend the man and lynch him." The correspondent placed the attack within a few miles of the Walker County community where, by the letter's account, a Black family had been killed and their house burned by a mob the previous summer.

At about 6 p.m. on Monday, May 26, Ed Morgan, 57, and his son Eddie Leroy Morgan, 17, were seized as they left the Huntsville post office, put into an automobile and driven two miles into the country. Before the mob left town, the city marshal reportedly told it, "If the girl identifies anybody tear his hide off." When the girl said neither man was the one she had seen, the mob prepared to whip the son, and after the father protested that he could punish his own son, it beat both. The elder Morgan, his face pressed into the mud, was beaten unconscious until 9:20 p.m.

The mob then brought George Mosely, a property owner and father of six, Levi Preston, and a son of the Baptist pastor Rev. James Franklin before the girl, who cleared each of them, and beat them as well. Some mob members called the girl "crazy" and vowed to beat Black men "until we get the right one." A "badly written sign" at the spot read, "We have beat 40 'niggers' on this spot and will beat 50 more." Before leaving, mob members warned Morgan that if he told what had been done they would "kill you and the whole damn family and burn the house down on you."

Morgan's wife summoned neighbors to lay him out, but he revived; he was greased, wrapped in a sheet and carried by wagon to another community, while she and an 8-year-old child walked seven miles through the woods to catch a train. The Informer reported that mob members stole Morgan's belongings, including a letter from the governor, and left uncertain the fate of his five acres of crops and his livestock. Huntsville's Black residents were described as "all excited," with many anxious to sell what they owned. The Informer said it held the names of several mob members, but no report of arrests or prosecution was found.

The attack is known chiefly from a single source, a special correspondent's letter from Huntsville dated June 1, which the Houston Informer printed on its front page on June 7 under the headline "HEATHEN, HELLISH, HUNNISH HUNTSVILLE'S HORRORS." The letter opened by calling Huntsville a "hell-hole," referred to the attackers as "Walker county hill-billies and roughnecks" and "Huns," and closed by contrasting a chief executive "3000 miles away from home" with conditions in the South: "The world can never be made safe for democracy as long as America is unsafe for its own citizens."

On June 13 the Baltimore Afro-American ran a shorter front-page story, datelined Huntsville, June 7, under the headline "FIVE BEATEN ONE DYING," with the subhead "Texas Mob Plays havoc with Colored Settlement." Its text compressed the Informer's details and quotations, naming only "Edward" and his son "Leroy," and added that the men's stock and farm implements had been confiscated.

The papers differ on details: the girl's age (16 in the Informer, 15 in the Afro-American), the sign's count (40 or 50), and whether a third victim was a minister or a minister's son. The Afro-American headline reported one victim "dying," while the Informer, the more detailed and closer source, reported that Morgan revived and mentioned no death.

reader.title: Huntsville mob beatings of May 1919
bases: A mob searching for an unidentified Black man seized and beat five Black men after the girl cleared each of them, threatening but not carrying out killing (A2, A3, A6).

The only detailed account is the Houston Informer's special correspondence (A2-A4); the Baltimore Afro-American story (A6), datelined on the Informer's issue date and repeating its details and quotations, appears to be a condensed version of it rather than an independent report.

accounts.label: Informer special correspondent
accounts.gist: Letter from Huntsville dated June 1: on May 26 a mob seized the Morgans at the post office, took them before the girl, who cleared them, and beat both, then beat three more cleared men; the mob threatened to kill the family and stole Morgan's belongings.

accounts.label: Afro-American summary
accounts.gist: A Huntsville-datelined condensed report that 'persons have been beaten by mobs' hunting the man the girl saw, naming Edward and his son Leroy, three other men, the sign, the marshal's words and confiscated stock.

accounts.label: Mob's statements as quoted
accounts.gist: Mob members were quoted vowing to beat every Black man in the community 'until we get the right one', and a sign at the spot claimed 40 (or 50) earlier beatings.

framing.detail: The Houston Informer ran the story under 'HEATHEN, HELLISH, HUNNISH HUNTSVILLE'S HORRORS', called the town a 'hell-hole' and the mob 'Huns', and closed by contrasting the president abroad with Americans 'unsafe' at home.
The Baltimore Afro-American ran a front-page news story headed 'FIVE BEATEN ONE DYING / Texas Mob Plays havoc with Colored Settlement', stressing the robbery of stock and personal effects.
